title.en: Section 1 - Enquiring about a Photography Course
title.zh: 第一部分 - 咨询摄影课程

sections.passage: A telephone conversation between a prospective student, Laura, and the administrator of a community education centre. Laura is interested in enrolling in a photography course. The administrator, Janet, provides details about the courses available. They offer three levels: Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced. The Beginner course runs for eight weeks, every Tuesday evening from 7 to 9 PM, and costs 180 pounds. It covers camera basics, composition techniques, and introductory editing using Adobe Lightroom. The Intermediate course is also eight weeks but on Thursday evenings and costs 220 pounds. Laura mentions she has some experience with photography as a hobby, having used a DSLR camera for about two years. Janet suggests she might be more suited to the Intermediate level, but recommends she attend a free assessment session next Monday at 6 PM to determine the most appropriate course. Laura asks about class sizes and Janet tells her that each class has a maximum of twelve students, which allows for plenty of individual attention from the tutor. The tutor for the Intermediate course is Mark Henderson, who is a professional photographer specializing in landscape and portrait photography. Janet mentions that students need to bring their own camera to class, but all other equipment, including lighting kits and backdrops, is provided. There is also a field trip included in the course fee — a visit to a local nature reserve for outdoor photography practice. Laura is also interested in the darkroom printing workshop, which is offered as a separate weekend course for 95 pounds. Janet gives Laura her email address to send the registration form and mentions that early registration discount of 10 percent is available if she signs up before the end of next week.

title.en: Section 2 - Tour of a New Community Library
title.zh: 第二部分 - 参观新社区图书馆

sections.passage: Welcome to the official opening tour of Meadowbrook Community Library. I'm Claire Robinson, the head librarian, and I'm delighted to show you around our brand new facility, which has been three years in the planning and construction. The library is located on the ground floor of the new Meadowbrook Cultural Centre and covers an area of 2,500 square metres. We have a collection of over 45,000 items, including books, audiobooks, DVDs, and digital resources. The library is divided into several distinct zones. The main lending area is on your left as you enter, and it houses our fiction and non-fiction collections arranged by genre and subject. To the right of the entrance is the children's library, which has been designed with young readers in mind. It features a story corner with colourful cushions and a small stage for storytelling events, which we plan to hold every Saturday morning at 10:30. The children's section has its own dedicated computer terminals with educational software. Moving further into the building, you'll find our reference and study area, which provides quiet study spaces for 60 people. We have 20 desktop computers available for public use, and free Wi-Fi throughout the building. The library also has four bookable meeting rooms that can accommodate groups of between 6 and 20 people. These can be reserved online or at the reception desk for a maximum of three hours per session. Our digital media lab is one of the most exciting features of the new library. It includes a recording studio, video editing suites, and a 3D printing facility. These resources are available to all library members, though training sessions are required before using the recording studio and 3D printers. The library is open Monday to Friday from 9 AM to 8 PM, Saturday from 9 AM to 5 PM, and Sunday from 11 AM to 4 PM. Library membership is free for all residents of the Meadowbrook district, and visitors can obtain a temporary membership for a fee of 5 pounds per day.

title.en: Section 3 - Discussion about a Group Project on Water Conservation
title.zh: 第三部分 - 关于节水小组项目的讨论

sections.passage: Two students, Alex and Mei, are discussing their group project for their Geography course. The project focuses on water conservation strategies in urban environments. Alex has been researching domestic water usage and has found some surprising statistics. He tells Mei that the average household in the UK uses approximately 350 litres of water per day, with the bathroom accounting for about 65 percent of total usage — roughly 30 percent for toilets, 25 percent for baths and showers, and 10 percent for taps. Mei has been looking at industrial water usage and discovered that manufacturing industries consume vast amounts of water, particularly the textile industry, which can use up to 200 litres of water to produce a single cotton T-shirt. They discuss how to present their findings effectively. Mei suggests creating a visual infographic to accompany their written report, which their tutor Dr. Patel has encouraged. Alex agrees and proposes dividing the project into four sections: domestic water usage, industrial water usage, existing conservation measures, and policy recommendations. For the third section on existing conservation measures, Mei has found that several cities have implemented innovative solutions. Singapore, for example, has developed NEWater, a system that treats and purifies reclaimed water to meet drinking water standards. The city of Windhoek in Namibia has been recycling wastewater for drinking purposes since 1968, making it a pioneer in water reclamation. In the UK, Thames Water has introduced smart metering that helps customers identify leaks and reduce consumption. For the policy recommendations section, Alex suggests focusing on three key areas: mandatory water-efficient fixtures in new buildings, incentive programmes for rainwater harvesting systems, and public education campaigns about water conservation. They agree to meet again next Wednesday to review their drafts and finalize the presentation. Their submission deadline is the 28th of November, and they plan to have a practice run of the presentation on the 25th.

title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于可持续农业的讲座

sections.passage: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture examines sustainable agriculture practices and their potential to address the growing challenge of feeding a global population projected to reach nearly 10 billion by 2050. Current agricultural methods, while highly productive, are placing enormous strain on the planet's resources. Agriculture currently accounts for approximately 70 percent of global freshwater withdrawals and occupies about 38 percent of the Earth's ice-free land surface. The intensive use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides has led to soil degradation, water pollution, and significant loss of biodiversity. One approach to more sustainable agriculture is organic farming, which avoids synthetic chemicals and emphasizes crop rotation, composting, and biological pest control. While organic farming typically produces lower yields than conventional agriculture — research suggests roughly 20 to 25 percent less on average — it has been shown to improve soil health over time and supports greater biodiversity. However, critics argue that widespread adoption of organic methods would require significantly more land to produce the same amount of food, potentially leading to further deforestation. Another promising approach is precision agriculture, which uses technology such as GPS-guided tractors, drone surveillance, and soil sensors to optimize the application of water, fertilizers, and pesticides. By applying inputs only where and when they are needed, precision agriculture can reduce chemical usage by up to 30 percent while maintaining or even increasing yields. Vertical farming, which involves growing crops in stacked layers within controlled indoor environments, represents a more radical departure from traditional agriculture. Vertical farms can operate year-round regardless of weather conditions, use up to 95 percent less water than conventional farming, and eliminate the need for pesticides entirely. However, the high energy costs associated with artificial lighting remain a significant barrier to scaling this technology. Perhaps the most innovative approach is the development of lab-grown meat and alternative proteins. Companies such as Impossible Foods and Beyond Meat have created plant-based products that closely mimic the taste and texture of animal meat, while others are developing cultured meat grown from animal cells. The livestock industry is responsible for approximately 14.5 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, so shifting toward alternative proteins could have a substantial impact on reducing agriculture's carbon footprint. In conclusion, no single solution will be sufficient to make agriculture truly sustainable. Instead, a combination of approaches, tailored to local conditions and supported by government policy, will be necessary to feed the world's growing population while protecting the planet's resources.

sections.passage:
Tea is the most widely consumed beverage in the world after water, with an estimated 3 billion cups consumed every day. Its history is deeply intertwined with the cultures of Asia and, eventually, the entire world. According to Chinese legend, tea was discovered in 2737 BC by the Emperor Shen Nung when leaves from a wild tea tree blew into his pot of boiling water. While this story is likely apocryphal, archaeological evidence suggests that tea drinking in China does indeed date back thousands of years. The earliest credible historical reference to tea dates to the 3rd century AD, in a medical text by the physician Hua Tuo.

During the Tang Dynasty, which ruled China from 618 to 907 AD, tea drinking became a sophisticated cultural practice. The scholar Lu Yu wrote The Classic of Tea, the first known monograph on tea, around 760 AD. This treatise codified the preparation and appreciation of tea, transforming it from a simple beverage into an art form. Tea was prepared by grinding dried leaves into a powder and whisking it with hot water — a method that bears a striking resemblance to the preparation of matcha tea in Japan today.

Tea was introduced to Japan by Buddhist monks who had traveled to China for study. The Japanese developed their own elaborate tea ceremony, known as chanoyu or sado, which elevated tea drinking to a spiritual practice emphasizing harmony, respect, purity, and tranquility. The ceremony was heavily influenced by Zen Buddhism and became one of the most distinctive aspects of Japanese culture. In the 16th century, the tea master Sen no Rikyu refined the ceremony into its current minimalist form, which is still practiced today.

European contact with tea began in the 16th century through Portuguese traders and missionaries who visited China and Japan. The Dutch East India Company began importing tea to Europe in 1610, and it quickly became fashionable among the wealthy elite. In Britain, tea drinking was popularized in the 17th century by Catherine of Braganza, the Portuguese wife of King Charles II. By the 18th century, tea had become Britain's national drink, and the British East India Company controlled a lucrative trade in tea from China.

The British appetite for tea had profound geopolitical consequences. The trade imbalance caused by Britain's massive tea imports led to the Opium Wars of the 19th century, as Britain sought to offset its trade deficit by selling opium grown in India to China. In an effort to break China's monopoly on tea production, the British botanist Robert Fortune was sent to China in 1848 to steal tea plants and learn the secrets of tea cultivation. Fortune successfully smuggled thousands of tea plants and seeds to India, where they were planted in the Darjeeling and Assam regions, establishing what would become a thriving Indian tea industry.

Today, the largest tea-producing countries are China, India, Kenya, and Sri Lanka. The global tea industry is worth over 50 billion dollars annually and supports the livelihoods of millions of workers worldwide, particularly in developing countries. Despite the rise of coffee culture in many parts of the world, tea remains deeply embedded in the cultural fabric of numerous societies and continues to be a source of comfort, connection, and contemplation for billions of people.

title.en: Passage 2 - The Rise of Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare
title.zh: 文章2 - 人工智能在医疗保健领域的崛起

sections.passage:
Artificial intelligence is transforming healthcare in ways that were unimaginable just a decade ago. From diagnosing diseases to discovering new drugs, AI technologies are being deployed across the medical field with remarkable results. However, this technological revolution also raises important questions about privacy, accountability, and the future role of human medical professionals.

One of the most promising applications of AI in healthcare is in medical imaging and diagnostics. Deep learning algorithms, trained on vast datasets of medical images, can now detect certain conditions with accuracy that matches or exceeds that of experienced radiologists. A landmark study published in the journal Nature in 2020 demonstrated that an AI system developed by Google Health could identify breast cancer in mammograms with fewer false positives and false negatives than human radiologists. Similarly, AI systems have shown exceptional performance in detecting diabetic retinopathy from retinal scans, skin cancer from photographs, and lung nodules from CT scans.

AI is also accelerating the process of drug discovery, which traditionally takes over a decade and costs billions of pounds. Machine learning algorithms can analyze molecular structures and predict how different compounds will interact with biological targets, significantly narrowing the field of potential drug candidates before expensive laboratory testing begins. In 2020, the AI company DeepMind made headlines when its AlphaFold system solved a 50-year-old grand challenge in biology by accurately predicting the three-dimensional structure of proteins from their amino acid sequence. Understanding protein structures is crucial for designing targeted drugs, and AlphaFold's achievement has been described as one of the most significant scientific breakthroughs of the 21st century.

In clinical settings, AI-powered tools are being used to assist doctors with treatment decisions. Clinical decision support systems can analyze a patient's medical history, current symptoms, and test results to suggest potential diagnoses and treatment plans. These systems can process far more information than any individual doctor, drawing on data from millions of patient records and the latest medical research. Some hospitals have implemented AI systems that monitor patients in real time, alerting medical staff to early signs of deterioration hours before human observation would detect them.

Despite these advances, the integration of AI into healthcare faces significant challenges. Data privacy is a major concern, as AI systems require access to large volumes of sensitive patient data to function effectively. There are also questions about transparency and explainability — many AI systems, particularly deep learning models, operate as black boxes, making it difficult for doctors and patients to understand how a particular diagnosis or recommendation was reached. This lack of transparency raises concerns about accountability when AI systems make errors. Furthermore, there is evidence that AI systems can perpetuate or amplify existing biases in healthcare. If the training data reflects historical inequities in medical treatment, the AI may produce recommendations that disadvantage certain demographic groups. Addressing these biases requires careful curation of training data and ongoing monitoring of AI system outputs.

sections.passage:
Music is a universal human phenomenon. Every known culture, from the most isolated tribal societies to the most technologically advanced nations, has some form of music. This universality has led scientists to speculate that the capacity for music may be hardwired into the human brain. Research over the past few decades has begun to reveal the complex ways in which music affects our brains, emotions, and behaviour, shedding light on why music is so central to human experience.

Neuroscience research has shown that listening to music activates more regions of the brain simultaneously than almost any other activity. Brain imaging studies reveal that music engages areas responsible for auditory processing, motor control, emotion, memory, and language. A particularly striking finding is that music triggers the release of dopamine, a neurotransmitter associated with pleasure and reward, in the brain's mesolimbic pathway — the same system activated by food, sex, and addictive drugs. This neurochemical response helps explain why music can be so intensely pleasurable and why people sometimes experience chills or goosebumps when listening to particularly moving passages.

The relationship between music and emotion has been extensively studied by psychologists. Research has consistently shown that music can induce a wide range of emotional states, from joy and excitement to sadness and nostalgia. Interestingly, the emotional impact of music appears to be largely independent of the listener's cultural background. A study published in the journal Nature in 2019 found that both Western listeners and members of the remote Mafa people of Cameroon could identify happy, sad, and fearful emotions in Western music, suggesting that some aspects of musical emotion recognition may be universal. However, the degree of emotional response does vary with cultural familiarity, with people generally experiencing stronger emotional reactions to music from their own cultural tradition.

Music also has powerful effects on cognitive performance, a phenomenon popularly known as the Mozart Effect. The original 1993 study by Rauscher, Shaw, and Ky found that college students who listened to Mozart's Sonata for Two Pianos in D Major for ten minutes showed temporarily improved spatial-temporal reasoning skills. While subsequent research has shown that the effect is modest and short-lived, the broader finding that music can influence cognitive function has been supported by numerous studies. Background music can improve performance on certain tasks, particularly those involving spatial reasoning, but it can also impair performance on tasks that require intense concentration and verbal processing, such as reading comprehension.

The therapeutic applications of music have also gained increasing recognition. Music therapy, which involves using music to address physical, emotional, cognitive, and social needs, has been shown to be effective in a variety of clinical settings. Research has demonstrated that music therapy can reduce anxiety and pain in surgical patients, improve communication skills in children with autism, and slow cognitive decline in patients with dementia. In a notable study at the University of Utah, researchers found that familiar music activated preserved neural pathways in patients with advanced Alzheimer's disease, temporarily restoring some cognitive function and emotional responsiveness.

The power of music extends beyond individual experience to social bonding. Singing and making music together has been shown to increase feelings of social cohesion and trust. A study at the University of Oxford found that group singing promotes the release of endorphins and synchronizes the heart rates and breathing patterns of participants, creating a powerful sense of connection and shared identity. This may explain why music has been a central feature of communal rituals, religious ceremonies, and military activities throughout human history.

text.zh: 最初的莫扎特效应研究是什么时候发表的？

text.en: When can music impair cognitive performance?
text.zh: 音乐什么时候会损害认知表现？

options.en: During tasks requiring intense concentration and verbal processing
options.zh: 在需要高度集中和语言处理的任务期间

text.en: What has music therapy been shown to reduce in surgical patients?
text.zh: 音乐疗法已被证明可以减少手术患者的什么？

text.en: What did the University of Utah study find about Alzheimer's patients?
text.zh: 犹他大学的研究对阿尔茨海默病患者发现了什么？

options.en: Music had no effect on their condition
options.zh: 音乐对他们的状况没有影响

options.en: Familiar music activated preserved neural pathways
options.zh: 熟悉的音乐激活了保留的神经通路
音乐加重了他们的症状

text.en: What does group singing promote according to Oxford research?
text.zh: 根据牛津大学的研究，群唱促进了什么？

options.en: Release of endorphins and synchronization of heart rates
options.zh: 内啡肽的释放和心率的同步

text.en: Which brain pathway is activated by music for pleasure?
text.zh: 音乐通过哪条脑通路产生愉悦感？

text.en: What is music therapy used for in children with autism?
text.zh: 音乐疗法对自闭症儿童有什么作用？

text.en: What physical responses does group singing synchronize?
text.zh: 群唱同步了什么身体反应？

text.en: What explains why music is central to communal rituals?
text.zh: 什么解释了音乐为什么是集体仪式的核心？

options.en: It increases social cohesion and trust
options.zh: 它增强了社会凝聚力和信任

options.en: It is required by religious doctrine
It was historically mandated by governments
options.zh: 历史上由政府强制要求

prompt.en: The diagram below shows the process of recycling plastic bottles. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features of the process. Write at least 150 words.
prompt.zh: 下面的图表展示了塑料瓶回收的过程。通过选择和报告该过程的主要特征来总结信息。至少写150个单词。

prompt.en: Some people believe that social media has a negative impact on society, while others think it has positive effects. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh: 一些人认为社交媒体对社会有负面影响，而另一些人则认为它有积极效果。讨论两种观点并给出你自己的意见。给出你回答的理由，并包括你自己的知识或经验中任何相关的例子。至少写250个单词。
